item.title: Lab 2: Memory Hierarchy and Caches
item.description:
Lab 2: Memory Hierarchy and Caches

This is the hands-on report for the lab in /home/sanketh/mem-lab on the Linux x86 laptop. It is the practical companion to content/posts/performance-engineering/2026-10-11-memory-and-caches.markdown — every experiment measures something the theory note claims, and a few go past it.

Same machine caveat as Lab 1: this is an Intel Core i5-8250U (15 W mobile part, base 1.6 GHz, max 3.4 GHz). It throttles under sustained load, so chase ratios, not absolute nanoseconds. All single-threaded timings below are pinned to one core with taskset -c 2.

item.title: Performance Engineering: Memory Hierarchy, Caches, and Data Layout
item.description:
Performance Engineering: Memory Hierarchy, Caches, and Data Layout

This note is the natural follow-up to the CPU microarchitecture note. There we saw that the CPU retires instructions as fast as it can and stalls when it cannot overlap work. For most programs, the dominant reason it cannot overlap work is memory: data is not where the CPU needs it, when the CPU needs it.

The goal here is to understand the cache hierarchy as a programmer sees it, how data layout controls cache behavior, and how to measure that behavior with the right tools.

item.title: The Page Tables
item.description:
Modern Linux Page Tables (4-Level Architecture)

Modern 64-bit processors require much larger address spaces, and the Linux kernel adapted by shifting to a 4-level (and more recently, a 5-level) page table architecture.

The Core Concept: Because a 64-bit address space is astronomically large and mostly empty, the kernel cannot use a single, massive translation array. Instead, it uses a hierarchical, multi-level tree of tables to map Virtual Addresses to Physical Addresses efficiently.
